## Today’s two-hour co-design cycle

| Time | Activity | What we make |
|---:|---|---|
| 00–12 | **1 · Experience check** | A completion poll + optional reflection |
| 12–35 | **2 · Map + rank** | Eight assessment areas + cohort priorities |
| 35–65 | **3 · Prepare + break** | One cohort priority + one disciplinary wildcard |
| 65–85 | **3 · Run** | Two separate five-minute runs + private owner notes |
| 85–108 | **3 · Exchange** | A partner reading + joint interpretation |
| 108–120 | **3 + 4 · Share + re-rank** | Five pair reports + a revised map |

::: {.plain-line}
**CORE:** bounded excerpt → two runs → independent reading → re-rank. **OPTIONAL slides: skip without loss.**
:::

::: {.notes}
- Keep this slide visible on arrival.
- With ten participants, form five pairs.
- If Oracle completion is low, Activity 1 becomes a brief poll only. Move directly to Activity 2 and use the recovered time for examples and setup.
:::

## What kind of workshop is this?

::: {.chain}
**CO-DESIGN THE MAP → PROTOTYPE PRESSURE → CO-READ THE TRACE → REVISE THE MAP**
:::

- Students identify **where** friction may matter.
- Students choose **how** to apply it.
- Students test it on their own material.
- Two readers interpret what happened.
- The cohort changes the framework from experience.

::: {.plain-line}
This is a **co-design workshop with a small co-research cycle**—not a validated study of learning effectiveness.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Participants are not simply receiving a finished framework. Their ranking, transcript readings, disagreements, and additions revise it.
- Do not call the room exercise research data unless a separate ethics, consent, governance, and analysis process exists.
:::

## Your role changes during the workshop

| Stage | Your role | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **1 · Experience** | **Learner** | Remember what receiving friction felt like. |
| **2 · Map** | **Teacher-designer** | Decide where pressure might support learning. |
| **3 · Test** | **Learner under test** | Answer first; after each STOP, record a private judgment. |
| **3 · Exchange** | **Peer examiner** | Examine the questioning—not your partner or their project. |
| **4 · Redesign** | **Co-researcher** | Compare perspectives and revise the shared framework. |

::: {.plain-line}
Role changes are deliberate. Do not grade yourself while you are answering.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Name each shift when it happens; participants should know which judgment they are being asked to make.
- “Peer examiner” means examiner of the interaction trace, not evaluator of the partner’s scholarship.
:::

## Activity 1 · Check the experience {.section-cover data-section="01 · EXPERIENCE CHECK" data-background-color="#174a34"}

**ROLE · LEARNER**

Start with what happened—or establish that it did not happen.

::: {.section-cover-detail}
Poll first → reflect only if there is enough shared experience
:::

::: {.notes}
- This is a decision gate, not a compliance check.
- No participant should have to explain why they did not complete the Oracle activity.
:::

## Anonymous completion poll {data-section="01 · EXPERIENCE CHECK"}

::: {.activity-label}
CHOOSE ONE · NO EXPLANATION REQUIRED
:::

1. **Completed** · I have a usable Oracle exchange.
2. **Started** · I used it, but do not have a usable exchange.
3. **Not yet** · I did not use it.

::: {.big-prompt}
If fewer than half the room has a usable exchange, we move directly to **Activity 2**.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Use an anonymous poll if available.
- Low completion is operational information, not failure.
- If completion is low, skip the next two slides. Everyone still participates fully using their own or supplied material later.
:::

## If we have enough experience · Remember the friction {data-section="01 · EXPERIENCE CHECK"}

Write privately:

1. **Where did the Oracle press?**
2. **What did it make you do before you could answer?**
3. **Did that help, miss the point, or become a barrier?**
4. **What might have been more worth pressing?**

::: {.plain-line}
The transcript records words. It may not show hesitation, irritation, relief, speech effort, or the urge to polish.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Give participants a brief private writing pause.
- A content-free answer is enough: “It made me distinguish my evidence from my conclusion.”
- Participants may pass and keep the reflection private.
:::

## Brief room round · What did friction do? {data-section="01 · EXPERIENCE CHECK"}

::: {.activity-label}
ONE OR TWO SENTENCES · YOU MAY PASS
:::

::: {.big-prompt}
Name one **thinking move** the pressure demanded—or one worthwhile move it failed to demand.
:::

Listen for:

**explain · compare · justify · connect · narrow · reconsider · contest · stop**

::: {.notes}
- Do not ask for research content.
- Capture verbs only. These verbs become a bridge to the eight assessment areas.
- If only a few participants completed the Oracle, take one or two examples and continue.
:::

## Activity 2 · Map and rank the areas {.section-cover data-section="02 · MAP + RANK" data-background-color="#174a34"}

**ROLE · TEACHER-DESIGNER**

Treat the eight areas like shared assessment lenses—not a finished grading rubric.

::: {.section-cover-detail}
Eight areas → individual ranking → cohort top three
:::

::: {.notes}
- The areas describe places where reasoning may need attention.
- They are broad enough to travel across history/theory, landscape, conservation, design, and other fields.
:::

## Eight areas where friction may matter {data-section="02 · MAP + RANK"}

::: {.chain}
**AREA → QUESTIONING TECHNIQUE → PEDAGOGICAL AIM → LLM QUESTIONS → TRACE**
:::

- An **area** is a part of the work worth examining.
- A **questioning technique** is how we invite examination there.
- A **pedagogical aim** names the thinking the learner should perform.
- The LLM generates the actual questions from the source and the learner’s answers.
- The transcript is evidence of what the technique actually produced.

::: {.plain-line}
These lenses organize attention. They do not prove that a student—or a piece of work—is weak.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Keep the language close to assessment practice: what are we looking at, what would count as evidence, and what question makes it visible?
- Avoid treating the area label as a verdict.
- A gap may emerge during questioning; the teacher-designer does not diagnose one in advance.
:::

## Areas 1–4 {data-section="02 · MAP + RANK"}

1. **Claim + evidence**  \
   Does the support fit the claim?

2. **Logic + assumptions**  \
   Why does one point lead to the next?

3. **Research method + design**  \
   Why this approach rather than another?

4. **Interpretation + alternatives**  \
   What else could explain or frame the material?

::: {.notes}
- Evidence may be archival, material, visual, observational, quantitative, testimonial, or practice-based.
- “Research method” includes scholarly, design, conservation, landscape, and pedagogical choices.
:::

## Areas 5–8 {data-section="02 · MAP + RANK"}

5. **Concept + measure**  \
   Does the indicator capture the idea?

6. **Scope + limits**  \
   Where does the claim stop applying?

7. **Perspective + position**  \
   Whose standpoint shapes—or is missing from—the account?

8. **Stakes + trade-offs**  \
   Who or what changes, benefits, loses, or carries the cost?

::: {.plain-line}
The framework remains open: add an area if the eight fail to hold something consequential.
:::

::: {.notes}
- “Concept + measure” includes qualitative indicators, categories, proxies, and interpretive criteria—not only numeric measurement.
- Perspective includes the researcher’s position, source position, affected groups, and disciplinary standpoint.
:::

## Rank the three that most deserve friction {data-section="02 · MAP + RANK"}

::: {.activity-label}
INDIVIDUAL RANKING · THEN POOL THE ROOM
:::

Rank three areas using both questions:

1. **How consequential is it if this reasoning is weak?**
2. **How easily could polished AI output hide the weakness?**

::: {.big-prompt}
Your #1 gets three points · #2 gets two · #3 gets one.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Use a ranking poll, sticky dots, or a shared board.
- Ask participants to rank for the teaching they realistically expect to encounter.
- Keep an “area missing” option beside the eight.
:::

## Read the first map {data-section="02 · MAP + RANK"}

Look at the cohort top three:

- What rose to the top—and why?
- Do different fields appear to value different areas?
- Is a low-ranked area less important, or merely harder to see?
- Did anyone name a missing area?

::: {.plain-line}
For today’s test, each person chooses **one cohort-priority area** and **one personal or disciplinary wildcard**.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Preserve the first ranking so it can be compared with the final ranking.
- Do not force consensus about why an area ranked highly.
- The wildcard must be a different area. It may sit outside the cohort top three when it matters to the participant’s field, teaching, or material.
:::

## Activity 3 · Test, exchange, and deliberate {.section-cover data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE" data-background-color="#174a34"}

Use one cohort priority and one disciplinary wildcard in separate bounded runs, then let another reader examine both traces.

::: {.section-cover-detail}
Teacher-designer → learner under test → peer examiner → co-researcher
:::

::: {.notes}
- This is the center of the workshop.
- Two short runs per person replace the earlier four-chat prompt comparison.
:::

## Pair setup · Hold the interface steady {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

In each pair:

1. Agree on the **same LLM interface and model**, where possible.
2. Each person will use **one fresh chat per area**.
3. Each person chooses **one cohort-priority area + one personal or disciplinary wildcard**.
4. Each person uses their **own safe source**.
5. Both follow the **same two-run protocol**: five minutes per area.

::: {.plain-line}
The tool does not need to be the Socratic Oracle. Use an LLM that can accept the test prompt.
:::

::: {.big-prompt}
[**OPEN THE COPY-READY DAY 2 LAB →**](day2-lab.html){target="_blank"}<br>
All techniques · brief · prompt · observation sheet
:::

::: {.notes}
- Pairing by interface reduces one obvious source of difference without pretending this is a controlled experiment.
- If exact models differ because of account access, record the difference rather than excluding anyone.
- The Oracle remains the experience source for Activity 1; its built-in questioning policy cannot be replaced by this custom test prompt.
- Keep the lab page open on participant devices so wildcard techniques remain available without returning the projected deck to every area slide.
:::

## Teacher-designer task · Choose where and how {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.chain}
**AREA → QUESTIONING TECHNIQUE → PEDAGOGICAL AIM → LLM GENERATES THE QUESTIONS**
:::

For each selected area, decide:

1. **Where:** Which part of the work deserves examination?
2. **How:** Which technique could prompt constructive thinking there?
3. **Why:** What thinking should the learner have to perform?
4. **Boundary:** What would make the pressure repetitive, leading, or misplaced?

::: {.plain-line}
**You choose the area, technique, and aim. You do not write the questions you will answer.**
:::

::: {.notes}
- “Challenge it” is not yet a questioning technique.
- A usable technique names the intellectual operation: justify, compare, connect evidence, test an alternative, set a boundary, or trace a consequence.
- The LLM generates the actual questions from the source and adapts them to the learner’s answers.
- Show the cohort-priority technique slides to the room. Participants use the copy-ready lab for a wildcard that is not among those projected.
:::

## Area: Claim + evidence · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">TRACE SUPPORT</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Which exact evidence supports each part of this claim?”

**Aim:** explicit links between evidence and claim—and what the evidence cannot support.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">TEST SUFFICIENCY</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What additional evidence would you need before making this claim?”

**Aim:** standards of adequacy, source quality, missing evidence, and uncertainty.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">INTRODUCE COUNTEREVIDENCE</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What evidence would weaken, narrow, or change your claim?”

**Aim:** willingness to revise and a clear threshold for changing position.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Claim + evidence is in the cohort top three.
- Evidence may be archival, material, visual, quantitative, testimonial, observational, or practice-based.
:::

## Area: Logic + assumptions · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">EXPLAIN THE BRIDGE</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Why does this evidence lead to that conclusion?”

**Aim:** the missing inferential step rather than a restatement of both ends.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">SURFACE AN ASSUMPTION</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What must be true for this reasoning to hold?”

**Aim:** hidden premises, dependencies, and conditions the writer can defend or revise.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">TEST AN ALTERNATIVE CHAIN</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Could the same evidence support a different conclusion? Compare the two.”

**Aim:** competing inferences and a reason for preferring one.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Logic + assumptions is in the cohort top three.
- A logic gap is not merely unclear wording; it is a missing or unsupported connection.
:::

## Area: Research method + design · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">JUSTIFY THE CHOICE</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Why is this method appropriate for this question?”

**Aim:** fit between question, evidence needed, method, and practical constraints.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">COMPARE AN ALTERNATIVE</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What would another plausible method reveal that this one might miss?”

**Aim:** genuine comparison rather than automatic defense of the original choice.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">TRACE METHOD TO CLAIM</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What can this method not establish—and which claim must therefore narrow?”

**Aim:** limitations that lead to a consequential change in claims.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Research method + design is in the cohort top three.
- “Method” includes scholarly, design, landscape, conservation, studio, and pedagogical methods.
:::

## Area: Interpretation + alternatives · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">GENERATE A RIVAL READING</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What is the strongest plausible alternative interpretation?”

**Aim:** an alternative that fits the material, not a token opposing view.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">SEEK DISCONFIRMING MATERIAL</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What observation or source would make you revise this interpretation?”

**Aim:** revision conditions and evidence the current reading cannot absorb.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">RESTORE CONTEXT</span>

**LLM may ask:** “How might the source’s genre, context, or purpose change this reading?”

**Aim:** historically and situationally grounded interpretation.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Interpretation + alternatives is in the cohort top three.
- Do not demand artificial balance when evidence strongly supports one interpretation.
:::

## Area: Concept + measure · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">DEFINE WHAT WOULD COUNT</span>

**LLM may ask:** “How would you know this concept is present in the material?”

**Aim:** observable or interpretable criteria rather than a circular definition.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">TEST CONCEPT–INDICATOR FIT</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What does this indicator capture—and what part of the concept does it miss?”

**Aim:** validity, proxy limits, ambiguity, and mismatch.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">TEST THE CATEGORY BOUNDARY</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Why does this example count, while a nearby case would not?”

**Aim:** thresholds, edge cases, and consistent classification.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Concept + measure is in the cohort top three.
- “Measure” may be quantitative, qualitative, visual, material, or interpretive.
:::

## Area: Scope + limits · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">FIND A BOUNDARY CASE</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Where would this claim stop applying?”

**Aim:** explicit conditions, populations, periods, sites, or cases.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">TEST TRANSFER</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Would this still hold in a different context? Why or why not?”

**Aim:** which mechanisms travel and which depend on local conditions.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">AUDIT THE GENERALIZATION</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What is the largest claim the current evidence can responsibly support?”

**Aim:** a narrower but defensible claim and stated uncertainty.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Scope + limits is in the cohort top three.
- Narrowing a claim is productive reasoning, not failure.
:::

## Area: Perspective + position · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">INTRODUCE A MISSING VIEWPOINT</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Whose account could change what is visible or important here?”

**Aim:** a consequential perspective, not decorative stakeholder listing.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">EXAMINE POSITION</span>

**LLM may ask:** “How does your—or the source’s—position shape what can be known?”

**Aim:** access, authority, distance, interest, and reflexive limits.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">TRACE SILENCE AND POWER</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Who can speak in this account, and whose absence affects the conclusion?”

**Aim:** structural absence, source conditions, and implications for interpretation.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Perspective + position is in the cohort top three.
- Do not ask participants to perform an identity or disclose personal experience.
:::

## Area: Stakes + trade-offs · Three techniques {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.method-stack}
::: {.method-card .method-a}
<span class="method-name">MAP CONSEQUENCES</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Who or what changes if this claim or proposal is acted upon?”

**Aim:** concrete effects, affected groups, material conditions, and time horizons.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-b}
<span class="method-name">DISTRIBUTE BENEFIT AND COST</span>

**LLM may ask:** “Who benefits, who carries the cost, and who decides?”

**Aim:** uneven distribution rather than one aggregate outcome.
:::

::: {.method-card .method-c}
<span class="method-name">TRACE A SECOND-ORDER EFFECT</span>

**LLM may ask:** “What could improve immediately while creating a later problem?”

**Aim:** unintended consequences, trade-offs, and delayed effects.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- Show this slide only if Stakes + trade-offs is in the cohort top three.
- Stakes can be ethical, social, environmental, cultural, economic, institutional, or pedagogical.
:::

## Worked example · What the teacher-designer chooses {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

> “The study will use interviews and confidence surveys to show that hybrid critique caused the improvement.”

**AREA 1 · COHORT PRIORITY · RESEARCH METHOD + DESIGN**  \
Questioning technique: **compare an alternative**  \
Pedagogical aim: make the learner compare what interviews and observation can establish

**AREA 2 · PERSONAL OR DISCIPLINARY WILDCARD · CLAIM + EVIDENCE**  \
Questioning technique: **trace support**  \
Pedagogical aim: make the learner distinguish association from evidence of causation

::: {.notes}
- The teacher-designer selects the area, technique, and intended constructive thinking—not an exact question.
- Both choices concern the same source but demand different reasoning.
:::

## Then the LLM performs the questioning {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| **Teacher-designer** | Supplies the area, questioning technique, and pedagogical aim. |
| **LLM questioner** | Reads the source, generates one grounded Socratic question, waits, then follows the learner’s actual answer. |
| **Learner** | Answers in their own words, contests false premises, and notices what the pressure does. |

::: {.big-prompt}
The question sequence is an **output being tested**, not something the learner must author in advance.
:::

::: {.notes}
- An acceptable first question might resemble a technique-menu example, but it must be grounded in the participant’s actual source.
- A follow-up should use something in the learner’s last answer rather than advancing through a canned checklist.
:::

## What a Socratic follow-up may do {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

| Move | Follow the last answer with… |
|---|---|
| **Clarify a term** | “What do you mean by ___ here?” |
| **Ask for the basis** | “What in the source or evidence makes you say that?” |
| **Expose an assumption** | “What must be true for that answer to hold?” |
| **Compare an alternative** | “How does that compare with ___?” |
| **Test a boundary** | “Would it still hold if ___ changed?” |
| **Trace a consequence** | “If that is true, what else must change?” |

::: {.plain-line}
The LLM chooses a follow-up from the **learner’s actual answer**. The learner does not pre-write it.
:::

::: {.notes}
- This helps participants recognize what the LLM is doing during the exchange and later examine it in the transcript.
- Every follow-up must use something the participant just said; it should not become a prewritten interrogation checklist.
- Stop early when the gap is sufficiently clear or the next question would only repeat pressure.
:::

## Choose a safe source {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

- **Core route · Bounded excerpt**  \
  A paragraph from an abstract, introduction, method, interpretation, or design statement.

- **Equal route · Supplied material**  \
  Use the fictional hybrid-studio paragraph.

::: {.safety-line}
Use only material you own or have permission to share with that service. Remove restricted, confidential, collaborator-controlled, or identifiable content.
:::

::: {.notes}
- A bounded excerpt is easier to compare and safer to exchange.
- Keep the bounded-excerpt route as the default even when an interface accepts files.
- A full-document route appears only in the optional appendix after the numbered workshop.
:::

## Copy prompt · Part 1 of 2: roles + inputs {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
COPY BOTH PARTS INTO ONE MESSAGE
:::

::: {.copy-prompt .test-template}
<span class="prompt-key key-role">YOUR ROLE · LLM</span> Be a Socratic questioner. Generate and adapt the questions; do not rewrite, solve, grade, or give me a verdict.

<span class="prompt-key key-role">MY ROLE · LEARNER</span> I will answer in my own words. Let me question, correct, or reject a false premise.

<span class="prompt-key key-source">SOURCE</span> [PASTE A SAFE BOUNDED EXCERPT—core route]

<span class="prompt-key key-area">AREA 1 · COHORT PRIORITY</span> [___]  \
<span class="prompt-key key-gap">TECHNIQUE 1 + PEDAGOGICAL AIM</span> [___]

<span class="prompt-key key-move">AREA 2 · PERSONAL / DISCIPLINARY WILDCARD</span> [___]  \
<span class="prompt-key key-question">TECHNIQUE 2 + PEDAGOGICAL AIM</span> [___]
:::

::: {.notes}
- Students replace every bracketed field: the source plus the two area and technique/aim pairs.
- The pedagogical aim comes from the technique card’s “Aim” line or a plain-language adaptation of it.
- The core prompt uses a bounded excerpt. Anyone taking the optional full-document extension must still name and paste the exact passage being examined.
:::

## Copy prompt · Part 2 of 2: Socratic rules {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
PASTE DIRECTLY AFTER PART 1
:::

::: {.copy-prompt .test-template}
Treat each area as a **focus for inquiry, not proof that a flaw exists**.

Use **one area per fresh chat**. Wait for **START AREA 1** or **START AREA 2**; use only that area.

For that area:

1. Read the source. Use the technique to ask one open, grounded question toward the aim.
2. Ask only that question; then wait.
3. Base each next question on my actual answer.
4. Stop by **five question–answer rounds**, or sooner if the aim is reached or pressure repeats.

On **STOP**, list only: reasoning I stated; one unresolved point; one exact response to revisit. **Never judge whether your questioning worked.** Then wait.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Students may adapt wording for their interface, but the pair should keep the role and interaction sequence equivalent.
- The area, technique, and pedagogical aim are the designed pressure; every actual question is model-generated output being tested.
- One exchange means one LLM question plus one participant answer. Five per area is a ceiling, not a quota.
- The LLM recap is part of the trace, not a verdict. Owner and partner evaluate the interaction independently.
:::

## Break · Then check the setup {data-section="BREAK"}

::: {.break-word}
PAUSE
:::

After the break, confirm:

**same LLM within the pair · two fresh chats per person · bounded source ready · cohort priority + wildcard chosen · aims stated**

::: {.notes}
- Protect the break.
- Use the final moments only for access and setup problems, not for judging anyone’s source.
:::

## Activity 3.1 · Two separate five-minute LLM runs {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
CURRENT ROLE · LEARNER UNDER TEST
:::

1. Open a fresh chat, paste the prompt, then type **START AREA 1**.
2. Stop designing. **Answer as a learner** for up to five exchanges.
3. At five minutes, type **STOP** and record a brief private owner judgment.
4. Open a second fresh chat, paste the prompt, then type **START AREA 2**.
5. Run another five minutes, type **STOP**, and record the second private judgment.

::: {.big-prompt}
Five exchanges are a **ceiling per run, not a target**. Stop early when an issue is clear. Each room timer wins.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Run two visible five-minute timers with a short private-note pause between them.
- Remind participants that their teacher-designer role is paused: they are now learners experiencing the question sequence.
- If the conversation stalls, answer “Please ask that more plainly” or contest the premise.
- Participants may stop early if the exchange becomes unsafe, irrelevant, or unproductive.
- Work individually and simultaneously. The purpose is to experience and observe pressure, not to produce a polished paragraph.
:::

## After each STOP · Record a private owner judgment {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
CURRENT ROLE · OWNER-OBSERVER · DO NOT SHARE YET
:::

Without reopening the exchange, note:

- one exact turn that **clarified or exposed** something;
- what thinking you had to perform;
- where the pressure **missed, overloaded, repeated, or became a barrier**; and
- your first judgment: **useful, partly useful, not useful, or still unclear**.

::: {.plain-line}
Keep this judgment private until the partner has finished an independent reading.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Give about one minute after each run. Participants can use ticks or short phrases.
- Separating answer time from judgment time protects the learner role and reduces simultaneous cognitive load.
- These are sensitizing prompts, not mandatory codes or a validated rating scale.
:::

## Stop, save, and prepare the handoff {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

Keep:

1. the two selected areas and questioning techniques;
2. the pedagogical aim for each;
3. a bounded packet containing the two short run transcripts; and
4. your private owner judgments—**held back for now**.

Redact names, sites, sensitive details, and anything your partner does not need.

::: {.safety-line}
The handoff contains the design brief and two redacted traces—**not** the private owner judgments, source document, account, chat link, or complete session.
:::

::: {.notes}
- The owner controls what is shared.
- Participants may provide a content-free summary or use the supplied case instead.
- The private judgments are revealed only after the partner records an independent reading.
:::

## Activity 3.2 · Trade transcripts {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
CURRENT ROLE · PEER EXAMINER OF THE INTERACTION
:::

::: {.swap-grid}
::: {.swap-side .swap-owner}
<span class="prompt-key key-role">OWNER HANDS OVER</span>

- two areas + techniques + aims;
- two bounded, redacted run traces;
- sharing limits.

**Hold back:** private owner judgments.
:::

::: {.swap-side .swap-partner}
<span class="prompt-key key-area">PARTNER READS</span>

- independently;
- against the same areas;
- with evidence from exact turns; and
- without seeing the owner’s judgments.
:::
:::

::: {.plain-line}
**Choose a handoff:** read on the owner’s device with no copy, or use a temporary redacted copy that is returned or deleted after comparison.
:::

::: {.safety-line}
Equal route: use the supplied traces or a content-free interaction packet. Personal disclosure is never required.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Both partners exchange at the same time.
- Owner-device reading is the default when practical. If a temporary copy is necessary, agree how it will be returned or deleted before exchanging it.
- No screenshots, forwarding, shared chat links, or retained copies after the discussion.
- The partner records an independent judgment before either person discusses the owner’s private memo.
:::

## Partner reading 1 · Did the intended pressure work? {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

For each selected area:

1. What constructive thinking was the teacher-designer trying to invite?
2. Did the LLM’s questions actually enact the chosen technique?
3. Did each follow-up use the learner’s preceding answer?
4. What thinking did the learner perform—and what became clearer?
5. Which exact turn supports your reading?

::: {.big-prompt}
Examine the **questioning design and interaction**—not the quality of the person or project.
:::

::: {.notes}
- The reviewer should be able to point to a question-and-response pair.
- “It was good” or “the bot was smart” is not enough.
:::

## Partner reading 2 · What else emerged? {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

Look beyond the intended areas:

- Did another gap become visible?
- Did the exchange demand more thinking—or only more words?
- Did it reveal an assumption, limit, perspective, or trade-off?
- Did pressure become generic, repetitive, misleading, or costly?
- Does the transcript suggest an area missing from the eight?

::: {.plain-line}
Record an additional area only when a specific turn gives you a reason.
:::

::: {.notes}
- This is the inductive part of the co-research cycle.
- The eight areas guide attention, but they do not get the last word.
:::

## Activity 3.3 · Reveal the independent readings {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
CURRENT ROLE · CO-RESEARCHER
:::

First, both confirm that the partner’s independent reading is recorded.

Then reveal in this order:

1. **Partner:** summarize the independent transcript reading.
2. **Owner:** reveal the private judgment recorded after STOP.

::: {.big-prompt}
The second perspective must exist **before** the first perspective is revealed.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Do not reveal the owner judgment until the partner note is complete; this protects the second perspective from avoidable anchoring.
- Neither reading is an answer key. The next slide asks the pair to compare them.
:::

## Compare the two readings {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
CURRENT ROLE · CO-RESEARCHER
:::

Compare without forcing agreement:

1. Where do the readings agree?
2. What did the partner see that the owner did not?
3. What does the owner correct, contest, or veto from experience or context?
4. Which area or questioning technique now looks more useful—and at what cost?

::: {.notes}
- Do not force agreement.
- The owner controls interpretations of their experience and research context; the partner can still retain a content-free methodological disagreement.
:::

## Make one joint co-research note {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

Complete together:

> We asked the LLM to use **[questioning technique]** within **[assessment area]** to invite **[constructive thinking]**. It was useful / partly useful / not useful because **[transcript evidence]**.

> The owner experienced **[effect or cost]**, while the second reader noticed **[pattern]**.

> Next time we would **[keep, change, remove, or test]** because **[reason]**.

::: {.plain-line}
Add one evidence-backed missing area or gap if the eight did not hold what emerged.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Keep the note content-free enough to share with the room.
- A failed questioning technique is a valid and useful result.
:::

## Activity 3.4 · Five-pair room round {data-section="03 · CO-RESEARCH CYCLE"}

::: {.activity-label}
CURRENT ROLE · CO-RESEARCHER
:::

Each pair shares:

1. **Area + questioning technique tested**
2. **One observed effect or failure**
3. **One difference between owner and partner readings**
4. **One change for the next version**

::: {.big-prompt}
Keep research content private. Share the **interaction pattern**. You may pass.
:::

::: {.notes}
- With five pairs, keep contributions concise.
- Record techniques, effects, disagreements, and proposed changes on a visible class atlas.
:::

## Activity 4 · Re-rank and redesign {.section-cover data-section="04 · RE-RANK" data-background-color="#174a34"}

**ROLE · TEACHER-DESIGNER + CO-RESEARCHER**

Return to the eight areas after the test—and allow the map to change.

::: {.section-cover-detail}
Second ranking → explain movement → name the next evidence needed
:::

::: {.notes}
- Reuse the same ranking mechanism and wording from Activity 2.
:::

## Rank the eight again {data-section="04 · RE-RANK"}

Use the same criteria:

1. **How consequential is it if this reasoning is weak?**
2. **How easily could polished AI output hide the weakness?**

Then ask:

- Which area moved up or down?
- Did its **importance** change—or did it become **easier or harder to assess**?
- Did the exercise reveal a ninth area?

::: {.big-prompt}
A ranking that does not move is also a result—if experience now gives you a reason.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Place the first and second maps side by side.
- Ask participants to explain change from evidence, not from a desire to appear reflective.
:::

## What did the co-design cycle change? {data-section="04 · RE-RANK"}

Compare:

| Before the test | After the test |
|---|---|
| What we expected to matter | What the exchange made consequential |
| What looked easy to assess | What produced usable transcript evidence |
| What the eight categories held | What they missed or blurred |
| What sounded like useful friction | What felt useful, costly, or off target |

::: {.plain-line}
The revised map is the cohort’s design artifact—not a universal hierarchy.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Preserve discipline-specific differences and contradictions.
- A category can be important yet difficult to test well with an LLM.
:::

## Leave with one redesigned friction point {data-section="04 · RE-RANK"}

- **Where:** one area that deserves attention;
- **How:** one questioning technique worth keeping or revising;
- **Evidence:** one transcript pattern that shaped the judgment;
- **Second perspective:** one difference the partner reading exposed; and
- **Next:** one thing a future workshop or study should test.

::: {.big-prompt}
Do not maximize friction. Co-design where it belongs, observe what it does, and revise the technique from more than one perspective.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Invite a final private note or voluntary spoken answer.
- Return or delete exchanged transcript packets before leaving.
:::

## OPTIONAL EXTENSION · SKIP WITHOUT LOSS {data-section="OPTIONAL EXTENSION"}

::: {.activity-label}
DESIGNING A NEXT STUDY · OUTSIDE THE CORE PATH · USE ONLY WHEN TIME REMAINS
:::

Today gives **interaction evidence**: questions asked, reasoning made visible, owner experience, a second-reader interpretation, and immediate changes or unresolved gaps.

It does **not** establish durable learning. A teaching study would still need:

**aligned work quality · comparison · retention · transfer · access and burden**

::: {.sources}
[Chi et al. (1994)](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1803_3) · [Deslauriers et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1821936116) · [Karpicke & Roediger (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1152408)
:::

::: {.notes}
- Optional extension: skip without loss. The numbered workshop ends on the preceding slide.
- Transcript evidence can show elicited reasoning, not durable learning.
- Feeling challenged and learning are related questions, not interchangeable measures.
:::

## OPTIONAL EXTENSION · SKIP WITHOUT LOSS {data-section="OPTIONAL EXTENSION"}

::: {.activity-label}
FULL-DOCUMENT CONTEXT · OUTSIDE THE CORE PATH · DO NOT USE FOR SETUP TROUBLESHOOTING
:::

Check all three:

1. **Service authorization:** The interface supports files and the relevant institutional setting permits this use.
2. **Material status:** The file is public, workshop-supplied, or a fully sanitized copy you are authorized to share.
3. **Scope:** You still identify one exact passage for the two runs.

::: {.big-prompt}
If any condition is uncertain, return to the bounded excerpt or supplied material. Nothing is lost.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Optional extension: skip without loss. It sits after the numbered workshop with the other appendix material.
- Acceptance by an interface does not establish institutional authorization, privacy, or collaborator permission.
- Never troubleshoot a personal full-file upload during this workshop. Return immediately to the bounded excerpt or supplied paragraph.
:::
